title: Anger, shed like a skin
hookLine: Lanka goes up in flames, and the monkey who lit it stands on the shore suddenly sick with one question: what if Sita burned too?
carry: krodha: shed anger like a snake's skin

cards: Hanuman leaps from rooftop to rooftop with his blazing tail, and the wind, his father, fans every flame. Mansions, towers and gateways catch fire. Valmiki describes Lanka burning like the end of an age.
Then Hanuman dips his tail in the sea, stops, and looks back. It's the moment after anger, when the heat drains away and a cold thought arrives: what did I just break?

teach.b: Valmiki notes one careful detail. Hanuman spares one house in all of Lanka: Vibhishana's, the brother who spoke up for him. Then the cold thought.
Sita. Did the fire reach the grove? Did I burn the very person I came to save?
Hanuman is horrified, and he turns on his own anger with words worth keeping. Blessed is the one who can throw off anger the moment it rises, the way a snake sheds its old skin.
An angry person can do anything: harm a teacher, say what should never be said. He calls himself a fool who has ruined Rama's whole mission in a moment of fury.
The hero of the Sundara Kanda, at the height of his triumph, condemns his own temper. This is a teaching Hindus hear again and again.
Anger, krodha, is counted among the six inner enemies, the shadripu, along with desire, greed, delusion, pride and envy: enemies you fight inside, not outside.
Then Hanuman hears the charanas, celestial beings, marveling in the sky: Lanka is burned, and yet Janaki, Sita, is unharmed.
Relief floods him, and he sees why: Sita is guarded by her own power.

teach.h: LIKE A SNAKE SHEDDING ITS SKIN.
teach.b: Fire, he reasons, does not burn fire.
He goes back one last time to the ashoka grove, sees her alive with his own eyes, bows, and takes his leave. He doesn't stay stuck in shame. He sheds the anger and goes to make sure she's safe.

how: Lanka-dahana, the burning of Lanka, is a beloved scene in Ramlila performances and temple art, and Hanuman's self-reproach over anger afterward is often quoted by teachers as a lesson in self-control.

games.q: you're Hanuman. Lanka is burning behind you, and you suddenly wonder if Sita was caught in it. what do you feel?
o: horror, and anger at your own anger.
games.why: Hanuman is horrified and condemns his rage, until signs and the charanas' voices tell him Sita is safe.

practice: Recall a recent moment of anger, small or large, and without reliving the argument, notice where you feel it in the body: jaw, chest, hands.
Breathe into that place, and on each breath out let the anger loosen and slip off, the way a snake slides out of an old skin. If you pray, say Rama's name softly as it goes.
Then, like Hanuman going back to the grove, think of one step to set things right.

wordCard.voice: The burning. Lanka set ablaze, Vibhishana's house spared, Hanuman's horror at his own anger, and the voices that tell him Sita is unharmed.

orig.note: Sanskrit krodha, anger: what Hanuman says should be shed like a snake's old skin.

carryVoice: Your line: krodha: shed anger like a snake's skin. Tomorrow, the leap home. Day six hundred twenty-nine.
